```{r setup, echo = FALSE}
library(lemur)
library(dplyr)

# helpers used by the display chunks and the prose facts below
cause_share <- function(cod, causes) {
  100 * sum(cod$deaths[cod$cause_name %in% causes]) / sum(cod$deaths)
}
lt_row <- function(lt, cod) c(
  e0     = lt$ex[lt$x == 0],
  q0     = lt$qx[lt$x == 0],
  l65    = lt$lx[lt$x == 65],
  e65    = lt$ex[lt$x == 65],
  deaths = sum(cod$deaths)
)

# facts quoted in the prose below
n_regions <- n_distinct(data_gbd_lt()$region)
n_causes  <- n_distinct(data_gbd_cod()$cause_name)
n_ages    <- n_distinct(data_gbd_lt()$x)
years     <- paste(range(as.numeric(levels(data_gbd_lt()$period))), collapse = " to ")
```

# What is lemur?

`lemur` ("Life expectancy monitor upscaled in R") is an R package and
Shiny application for scenario analysis of mortality. Given the cause-of-death
distribution of a population, you ask *"what if?"* questions -- *what would
life expectancy be if cardiovascular mortality fell by 50%?* -- and the
package recomputes the life table, shows you the gains and losses at every
age, and decomposes the change by age and cause of death. It also compares
cause-of-death profiles and life tables between regions, sexes and time
periods.

Everything runs on the bundled Global Burden of Disease 2023 (GBD 2023)
estimates from IHME: `r n_regions` regions from `r years` (the
calendar-year-2023 data included), three sex categories (male, female and the
two sexes combined) and `r n_causes` broad cause groups, arranged in abridged
life tables of `r n_ages` age groups.

The tool is hosted by the **HASS Digital Research Hub (HDRH)** at the
Australian National University (ANU).

# Installation

Once you have an R session open (in RStudio or the R console), install the
package straight from [GitHub](https://github.com/mpascariu/lemur):

lemur requires **R version 4.3.0 or newer**.

``` r
# 1. Install the pak package, if you do not have it yet
install.packages("pak")

# 2. Install lemur from GitHub (latest version on the main branch)
pak::pak("mpascariu/lemur")
```

The package bundles the GBD 2023 datasets (exposed as `data_gbd_lt()`,
`data_gbd_cod()` and `data_gbd_sdg()`), covering deaths and life tables from
1990 to 2023, so you can run the examples on the help pages and the analysis
functions without a database connection.

# The data

The three accessor functions return pre-factorized `data.table`s:

* `data_gbd_lt()` -- one abridged life table per region, sex and year,
  with the classic columns `mx`, `qx`, `ax`, `lx`, `dx`, `Lx`, `Tx` and `ex`.
* `data_gbd_cod()` -- death counts by region, sex, year, age group and
  cause (`deaths` column).
* `data_gbd_sdg()` -- the same, grouped into the cause categories used
  for tracking the UN Sustainable Development Goals.

Let's look at Romania in 2021 (both sexes combined). An excerpt of the life
table -- survivors `lx`, deaths `dx`, probability of dying `qx` and remaining
life expectancy `ex` -- at selected ages:

```{r lt-excerpt}
library(lemur)

# helper used throughout this document, defined at first use
slice_table <- function(tbl, region, sex = "both", year = 2021) {
  filter(tbl, region == .env$region, sex == .env$sex, period == .env$year)
}

lt_ro  <- slice_table(data_gbd_lt(), "Romania")
cod_ro <- slice_table(data_gbd_cod(), "Romania")
cardio <- c("Ischemic Heart Disease", "Stroke", "Other Cardiovascular")
total_deaths <- sum(cod_ro$deaths)
```

```{r lt-excerpt-table, echo = FALSE}
lt_ro %>%
  filter(x %in% c(0, 1, 10, 20, 40, 60, 80, 100)) %>%
  select(x.int, x, mx, qx, lx, dx, ex) %>%
  mutate(across(c(mx, qx), ~ round(.x, 5)),
         across(c(lx, dx), ~ format(round(.x), big.mark = ",")),
         ex = round(ex, 2)) %>%
  knitr::kable(format = "html")
```

Life expectancy at birth in Romania in 2021 was
**`r round(lt_ro$ex[lt_ro$x == 0], 2)` years**, with
`r format(round(lt_ro$lx[lt_ro$x == 65]), big.mark = ",")` of every 100,000
newborns surviving to age 65. The corresponding cause-of-death table counts
`r format(total_deaths, big.mark = ",")` deaths in that year, distributed
over `r n_causes` causes and `r n_ages` age groups.

```{r cod-slice, echo = FALSE}
cod_by_cause <- cod_ro %>%
  group_by(cause_name) %>%
  summarise(Deaths = sum(deaths)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(Share = round(100 * Deaths / total_deaths, 1)) %>%
  arrange(desc(Deaths))

top_cause     <- cod_by_cause$cause_name[1]
top_share     <- cod_by_cause$Share[1]
cardio_before <- round(cause_share(cod_ro, cardio), 1)

cod_by_cause %>%
  head(8) %>%
  knitr::kable(format = "html", digits = 1)
```

The largest single block -- `r top_cause` -- accounts for `r top_share`% of
all deaths. (2021 was a pandemic year, so COVID-19 tops the list.) This is
the kind of target a scenario analysis will aim at.

# Workflow I -- "What if" scenario analysis

The core idea: mortality at age *x* from cause *c* can be reduced or
increased by a factor, and the all-cause life table is rebuilt from the
modified cause-specific risks. This is what the Shiny app does every time you
move a slider, and the same functions are exported for use in scripts.

The pipeline has three steps:

1. `build_cod_matrix()` turns the long cause-of-death table into an
   age × cause matrix of death *shares* (each row sums to 1).
2. `modify_cod_table()` (or `modify_life_table()`) applies a percentage
   change -- as a scalar, a vector, or a full age × cause matrix.
3. The modified risks are converted back into a life table.

Let's model a realistic question: **what if cardiovascular mortality in
Romania in 2021 were halved, at every age?** In the GBD classification,
cardiovascular deaths are split across three cause groups -- ischaemic heart
disease, stroke and other cardiovascular -- together worth
`r cardio_before`% of all deaths. The change is a matrix of zeros with -50 in
the three cardiovascular columns:

```{r scenario}
causes <- as.character(unique(cod_ro$cause_name))
ages   <- unique(lt_ro$x)

M <- matrix(0, nrow = length(ages), ncol = length(causes),
            dimnames = list(ages, causes))
M[, cardio] <- -50

scenario <- prepare_data(
  cod = cod_ro, lt = lt_ro,
  region1 = "Romania", region2 = "Romania", sex = "both",
  cod_change = M, mode = "cod"
)
lt_after  <- scenario$lt_final
cod_after <- scenario$cod_final
```

```{r scenario-facts, echo = FALSE}
# numbers quoted in the prose below
e0_before    <- lt_ro$ex[lt_ro$x == 0]
e0_after     <- lt_after$ex[lt_after$x == 0]
gain_e0      <- round(e0_after - e0_before, 2)
deaths_saved <- round(total_deaths - sum(cod_after$deaths), -3)
cardio_after <- round(cause_share(cod_after, cardio), 1)

# remaining life expectancy gained at age x
gain_at <- function(age)
  lt_after$ex[lt_after$x == age] - lt_ro$ex[lt_ro$x == age]
```

`prepare_data()` is the exact function the app runs: it filters the inputs,
applies the change and returns the initial and final life tables and
cause-of-death tables. The result:

```{r scenario-summary, echo = FALSE}
rows_before <- lt_row(lt_ro, cod_ro)
rows_after  <- lt_row(lt_after, cod_after)

data.frame(
  Indicator = c("Life expectancy at birth (years)",
                "Probability of death before age 1",
                "Survivors to age 65 (per 100,000)",
                "Life expectancy at 65 (years)",
                "Total deaths (all causes)"),
  Before = c(round(rows_before[["e0"]], 2),
             round(rows_before[["q0"]], 4),
             round(rows_before[["l65"]]),
             round(rows_before[["e65"]], 2),
             format(round(rows_before[["deaths"]]), big.mark = ",")),
  After = c(round(rows_after[["e0"]], 2),
            round(rows_after[["q0"]], 4),
            round(rows_after[["l65"]]),
            round(rows_after[["e65"]], 2),
            format(round(rows_after[["deaths"]]), big.mark = ","))
) %>%
  knitr::kable(format = "html")
```

Life expectancy at birth rises by **`r gain_e0` years** (`r round(e0_before, 1)`
→ `r round(e0_after, 1)`), and roughly `r format(deaths_saved, big.mark = ",")`
fewer deaths occur in a year. Note that the *deaths* drop by about half of
the cardiovascular deaths -- the other causes are untouched.

Where does this gain in life expectancy come from? `plot_change()` plots the
remaining life expectancy of the first life table minus the second at every
age: a marker to the right of the dashed zero line is a gain, a marker to the
left a loss.

```{r fig-change, fig.cap = "Age-specific gains in remaining life expectancy from halving cardiovascular mortality (Romania, 2021)."}
plot_change(L1 = lt_after, L2 = lt_ro,
            title = "Halving cardiovascular mortality: gains by age",
            subtitle = "Romania, 2021, both sexes")
```

The gains are strikingly uniform: halving cardiovascular mortality adds
`r round(gain_at(0), 2)` years of remaining life expectancy at birth,
`r round(gain_at(30), 2)` at age 30, `r round(gain_at(60), 2)` at 60 and
still `r round(gain_at(80), 2)` years at 80, before tapering to
`r round(gain_at(100), 2)` at age 100. Because the reduction applies
proportionally at *every* age, the saved person-years accrue to the whole
population rather than piling up in old age; the gain fades only where little
life remains to be gained. The cause-of-death profile after the change tells
the other half of the story:

```{r fig-cod, fig.cap = "Cause-of-death profile of Romania 2021 (both sexes), after a 50% reduction of cardiovascular mortality."}
plot_cod(cod_after, perc = TRUE)
```

Compare this with the initial distribution: the cardiovascular share of all
deaths falls from `r cardio_before`% to `r cardio_after`%. Every other cause
keeps its death count exactly -- only the three cardiovascular columns
changed. That is the "what if" contract: a small set of levers moved,
everything else held constant.

Finally, we can *decompose* the `r gain_e0`-year gain into age-by-cause
contributions with `decompose_by_cod()` and draw the result with
`plot_decompose()`:

```{r fig-decomp-scenario, fig.cap = "Decomposition of the life-expectancy gain: contribution of each cause at each age (stacked bars, positive above the zero line)."}
dec_scenario <- decompose_by_cod(lt_ro, lt_after, cod_ro, cod_after)
plot_decompose(dec_scenario, by = "both")
```

```{r peak-sc, echo = FALSE}
peak_sc <- dec_scenario %>%
  group_by(x.int) %>%
  summarise(contribution = sum(decomposition)) %>%
  slice_max(contribution, with_ties = FALSE)
```

As expected, the entire gain is attributed to the three modified causes.
Positive values favor the second population passed -- here the post-change
table -- which is why the whole figure lies above the zero line. The stack
shows the *age pattern*: the age group contributing the most is
`r peak_sc$x.int` (`r round(peak_sc$contribution, 2)` years), the ages where
cardiovascular deaths are concentrated. Each bar is the sum of the per-cause
contributions, and the sum of the whole figure equals the total gain to the
last decimal.

# Workflow II -- decomposing differences between populations

The same toolkit answers *comparative* questions: **why does male life
expectancy differ between Romania and Mexico in 2021?** First, the gap:

```{r compare}
lt1  <- slice_table(data_gbd_lt(), "Romania", sex = "male")
lt2  <- slice_table(data_gbd_lt(), "Mexico",  sex = "male")
cod1 <- slice_table(data_gbd_cod(), "Romania", sex = "male")
cod2 <- slice_table(data_gbd_cod(), "Mexico",  sex = "male")
```

```{r compare-facts, echo = FALSE}
e0_1 <- lt1$ex[lt1$x == 0]
e0_2 <- lt2$ex[lt2$x == 0]
gap  <- e0_2 - e0_1
```

Male life expectancy at birth is `r round(e0_1, 2)` years in Romania and
`r round(e0_2, 2)` years in Mexico -- a gap of **`r round(abs(gap), 2)` years**,
favoring `r if (gap > 0) "Mexico" else "Romania"`. `decompose_by_age()` splits
this gap into age contributions (using the direct-indirect method of Andreev,
Shkolnikov and Begun, 2002):

```{r age-dec}
dec_age <- decompose_by_age(lt1, lt2)
```

```{r age-dec-table, echo = FALSE}
best  <- dec_age[which.max(dec_age$decomposition), ]
worst <- dec_age[which.min(dec_age$decomposition), ]

dec_age %>%
  select(x.int, decomposition) %>%
  mutate(decomposition = round(decomposition, 3)) %>%
  knitr::kable(format = "html")
```

The sign convention is simple: positive values favor the second population
passed to the function -- here Mexico -- and negative ones favor the first
(Romania). The age pattern shows where the advantage is won and where it is
lost: the `r best$x.int` age group contributes the most in Mexico's favor
(`r round(best$decomposition, 3)` years), while the `r worst$x.int` group
works the other way (`r round(worst$decomposition, 3)` years, favoring
Romania). The column sums exactly to the total gap.

`decompose_by_cod()` refines this by cause, using stepwise replacement: it
replaces the mortality of one population with the other's, cause by cause and
age by age, and reads off the life-expectancy effect of each replacement.
The `symmetrical = TRUE` (default) and `direction = "up"` arguments follow
the recommendations of Andreev et al. (2002), averaging the two replacement
directions.

```{r cod-dec}
dec <- decompose_by_cod(lt1, lt2, cod1, cod2)
```

```{r cod-dec-table, echo = FALSE}
by_cause <- dec %>%
  group_by(cause_name) %>%
  summarise(contribution = sum(decomposition)) %>%
  ungroup()

top_abs <- which.max(abs(by_cause$contribution))
top_pos <- which.max(by_cause$contribution)

by_cause %>%
  mutate(contribution = round(contribution, 3)) %>%
  arrange(desc(abs(contribution))) %>%
  head(6) %>%
  knitr::kable(format = "html")
```

In absolute terms the largest single contribution is
`r by_cause$cause_name[top_abs]` (`r round(by_cause$contribution[top_abs], 2)`
years, in Romania's favor): Mexico's male COVID-19 mortality in 2021 far
exceeds Romania's. The largest factor pulling the other way is
`r by_cause$cause_name[top_pos]` (`r round(by_cause$contribution[top_pos], 2)`
years, in Mexico's favor) -- Romanian males' stroke mortality sits well above
Mexico's. The full picture -- each cause at each age -- is best seen in the
stacked plot:

```{r fig-decomp-cmp, fig.cap = "Decomposition of the male life-expectancy gap between Romania and Mexico, 2021: contributions by cause and age."}
plot_decompose(dec, by = "both")
```

Reading the bars: segments above the zero line favor the second population
(Mexico), segments below favor the first (Romania). The colours follow the
package-wide cause palette, so the same cause carries the same colour in
every figure. Summing every segment recovers the total gap to the last
decimal -- the decomposition is exact, not an approximation.

Cause-of-death *differences* can also be viewed directly with `plot_cod()`
in comparison mode, or collapsed to a single horizontal bar with
`plot_decompose(by = "cod")`:

```{r fig-decomp-cod, fig.cap = "The same decomposition collapsed to one horizontal bar per cause."}
plot_decompose(dec, by = "cod")
```

# The Shiny application

Everything above is wrapped in an interactive dashboard, launched with a
single call:

``` r
lemur::run_app()          # local data mode (bundled GBD data)
```

```{r app-screenshot, echo = FALSE, fig.cap = "The interactive dashboard, launched with lemur::run_app()."}
knitr::include_graphics(system.file("app/www/app_lemur_20260812.png", package = "lemur"))
```

The dashboard offers five analysis modes:

| Mode | Question it answers |
|------|---------------------|
| Scenario (within region) | What if a set of causes is reduced in one region? |
| Region comparison | How do two regions differ, and why? |
| Sex comparison | What explains the male-female gap in one region? |
| SDG targets | What if the UN SDG targets on premature mortality were met? |
| SDG by cause | The same, with finer per-cause controls |

In every mode, moving a slider or ticking a cause re-runs the pipeline shown
above; a 250 ms debounce batches input changes into a single consistent
update, cached reactives avoid recomputing unchanged queries, and all charts
render natively in plotly (roughly 0.1 s per interaction). A "Data" tab
exposes the underlying tables -- initial and final life tables, death counts,
the decomposition and the reduction matrix -- and the "Methods" tab explains
the algorithms. The map tab shows the selected region on an interactive
leaflet map with 2021 population, life expectancy and fertility indicators.

The SDG modes use the bundled `data_gbd_sdg()` table, which groups the
same death counts into the SDG cause categories:

```{r sdg-slice, echo = FALSE}
slice_table(data_gbd_sdg(), "Romania") %>%
  group_by(cause_name) %>%
  summarise(Deaths = sum(deaths)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  arrange(desc(Deaths)) %>%
  knitr::kable(format = "html", digits = 0)
```

This makes it easy to ask, for instance, how much life expectancy would
improve if the SDG 3.4 target -- a one-third reduction of premature mortality
from non-communicable diseases -- were achieved in a given region.

# References

* Every exported function has a worked example: `?modify_life_table`,
  `?decompose_by_cod`, `?plot_decompose`, `?data_gbd_lt`.
* The decomposition methods follow Andreev, Shkolnikov and Begun (2002),
  *Algorithm for decomposition of differences between aggregate demographic
  measures*, Demographic Research 7, 499-522.
* The data are the Global Burden of Disease Study 2023 (GBD 2023) results,
  Institute for Health Metrics and Evaluation (IHME)
  (<https://vizhub.healthdata.org/gbd-results/>). The calendar-year-2023 data
  is included; deaths and life tables span 1990-2023.
* Source code, issues and releases: <https://github.com/mpascariu/lemur>.
